02.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
02.event: They meant to let a nursing widow marry right away on the strength of a baraita, but an old woman objected that Rav Nachman had forbidden her.
02.turn: Rav Pappi showed them a baraita and a ruling of Rabbi Meir that they had overlooked, which undercut the leniency.
02.outcome: They admitted they had not had that in mind, and the rule was set that if the child died she may marry and if she weaned it she may not.
02.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna were about to permit a nursing woman to remarry at once, following a baraita. An old woman told them Rav Nachman had forbidden it in her own case. Rav Pappi then cited a baraita and a ruling of Rabbi Meir, and they conceded they had not thought of it. The rule was then fixed, and a story of a woman who strangled her child was dismissed as the act of an insane woman.

04.actor: Rav Acha bar Abba and his son-in-law Rav Chisda
04.event: Rav Acha visited Rav Chisda and sat his granddaughter on his lap, and they traded charges that each had broken a ruling of Rav or Shmuel.
04.turn: Rav Chisda objected that she might be betrothed, Rav Acha said that would mean Rav Chisda had broken Rav's ruling, and Rav Chisda then pointed out that holding her broke Shmuel's ruling.
04.outcome: Rav Acha answered with another statement of Shmuel that such acts done for the sake of Heaven are permitted.
04.summary: Rav Acha bar Abba visited his son-in-law Rav Chisda and sat his granddaughter on his lap. Rav Chisda asked whether she might already be betrothed. Rav Acha replied that if so Rav Chisda had broken a ruling of Rav. Rav Chisda then said Rav Acha had broken Shmuel's ruling against using a woman, and Rav Acha answered with another ruling of Shmuel that everything done for the sake of Heaven is permitted.

05.actor: Reish Lakish, Rabbi Yochanan, and judges
05.event: Judges ruled in a case according to Rabbi Tarfon and Reish Lakish overturned their ruling and restored the money to the heirs.
05.turn: Rabbi Yochanan criticized Reish Lakish for treating the error as one that must be reversed as in a Torah-law ruling.
05.outcome: The story ends with Rabbi Yochanan's rebuke, and the Gemara then discusses what they disagreed about.
05.summary: Some judges decided a case of seized produce according to Rabbi Tarfon. Reish Lakish reversed their decision and gave the money to the heirs, following Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yochanan told him he had acted as if it were a Torah-law matter.
05.missing: The case itself is not described, and the dispute with Rabbi Yochanan is left open here.

06.actor: Rav Chiyya Arikha and his brother's widow
06.event: After supporting his brother's widow for twenty-five years in her father's house, he refused her demand for sustenance and then for her marriage contract, and she took him to court.
06.turn: Rabba bar Sheila ruled that she could still collect and gave her a document to seize his property. Rav Chiyya went to Rava, who said the ruling was sound, but the document lacked a needed clause.
06.outcome: Rava ruled the document was defective, so she got no produce. Even Rabba bar Sheila had erred in leaving the clause out.
06.summary: Rav Chiyya Arikha supported his brother's widow for twenty-five years, and she then demanded sustenance and her marriage contract. He refused, and she took him to Rabba bar Sheila, who ordered him to pay and gave her a document to seize his property. Rav Chiyya complained to Rava, who said the judgment was right. The widow then asked for the produce, and Rava said the document was defective and she was not entitled to it, because it lacked a clause identifying the property as her husband's.

07.actor: A man whose mother had been taken captive with him, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
07.event: A man spoke offhandedly about how he and his mother had been captured and how his thoughts stayed with her while he drew water and gathered wood.
07.turn: His remark was an unguarded one and not formal testimony, and a son is normally disqualified from testifying for his mother.
07.outcome: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi accepted it and allowed her to marry a priest.
07.summary: A man came before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and said in passing that he and his mother had been captured, and that his thoughts were always on her whether he went to draw water or gather wood. Rabbi accepted this casual remark as evidence that she had not been defiled and let her marry into the priesthood.

08.actor: The neighbors of a gentile superintendent, and Rabbi Zeira
08.event: A gentile superintendent refused to rent his domain to his Jewish neighbors for an eiruv, so they asked Rabbi Zeira whether they could rent it from his wife.
08.turn: Rabbi Zeira cited a teaching of Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Chanina that a wife may establish an eiruv without her husband's knowledge.
08.outcome: On that basis the neighbors could rent the domain from the wife.
08.summary: A gentile superintendent living near Rabbi Zeira would not rent his domain to his neighbors so they could carry on Shabbat. They asked Rabbi Zeira whether they could rent it from his wife. He told them Rabbi Chanina had taught that a man's wife may establish an eiruv without his knowledge, so they could.

09.actor: Ravina and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
09.event: Ravina found Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak leaning on a doorpost and puzzling over what the law is if a husband says only that a get is void.
09.turn: The question could not be answered.
09.summary: Ravina found Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak leaning on a doorpost, deep in thought over whether a husband who says only that a get is void has cancelled it. No answer was found and the question was left standing.
09.missing: Nothing really happens beyond finding him thinking, and no resolution is given.

10.event: Levi taught the rule that a get written on forbidden-benefit material is valid, first in the name of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and then in the name of the majority.
10.turn: The first time his hearers did not praise him, and the second time they did.
10.outcome: From this the Gemara concluded that the law follows Rabbi.
10.summary: Levi went out and taught a ruling in the name of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and the audience did not praise him. When he taught the same ruling in the name of the majority, they praised him. The Gemara took this as a sign that the halakha follows Rabbi.

11.actor: Rabbi Chelbo, Rabbi Avira, Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina, and later Rabbi Elazar
11.event: Three sages visiting a place were served a peach as big as a five-se'a stewpot and they ate a third, abandoned a third and fed a third to their animals. The next year Rabbi Elazar visited and was served a peach small enough to hold in one hand.
11.turn: The fruit had shrunk, and Rabbi Elazar quoted a verse blaming the sins of the inhabitants.
11.outcome: He took the shrunken peach as a sign that a fruitful land had turned barren because of its people's wickedness.
11.summary: Three sages visiting a certain place were served a gigantic peach, so large that they ate a third, gave a third to their animals, and left a third ownerless. A year later Rabbi Elazar visited, and was given a peach he could hold in one hand. He quoted the verse about a fruitful land turned to salt because of the wickedness of those who live there.

12.actor: A debtor, Rav Pappa and Rav Chama
12.event: Rav Pappa asked for the actual case behind a ruling attributed to Rava, and Rav Chama described a debtor who tried to hide his money by claiming it belonged to a gentile.
12.turn: The man acted improperly, and so the sages treated him improperly by making him sell his land.
12.outcome: The ruling applied only to that kind of debtor.
12.summary: Rav Pappa asked Rav Chama whether Rava had really ruled that a debtor with land must sell it to pay. Rav Chama said that was not the ruling, and that the case had involved a debtor who pretended his money belonged to a gentile. Because he acted improperly, the sages forced him to sell his land.
12.missing: The debtor's own acts and the court's action are only described briefly in the retelling of a past case.

13.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
13.event: Rabbi Yehoshua visited Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri to learn, found him sitting among trees, stretched a vine from one tree to another, and asked about sowing in the enclosed area.
13.turn: He was told it was permitted if the trees were ten cubits apart and forbidden if more.
13.outcome: The reply showed the distinction between ten cubits and more than ten, and the Gemara used it to resolve a contradiction.
13.summary: Rabbi Yehoshua came to study with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and found him sitting among trees. He stretched a vine between two trees and asked whether he could sow diverse kinds in the area on the far side of it. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri said that it was permitted if the trees were ten cubits apart and forbidden if they were farther apart.
13.missing: There is no real turn, and the account is used as a source for a legal distinction.

14.actor: A dying man's heirs and his daughter
14.event: A man left his daughter a palm tree in his will, and the heirs divided the estate without giving her one.
14.turn: Rav Yosef thought this was like the mishna's case where each heir can say the tree is in another's share, but Abaye said it was different because the tree is in all their hands.
14.outcome: Abaye ruled they must give her a palm tree and redivide the estate.
14.summary: A man told his heirs to give his daughter a palm tree, but they split the property and gave her none. Rav Yosef compared the case to a mishna in which each owner can fend off a claim, but Abaye said the cases differ since the tree is held by all of them. His remedy was to give her a tree and divide the estate again.
14.missing: The heirs' behavior and the daughter's response are barely described.

15.actor: A launderer who regularly visited Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
15.event: On the day Rabbi died a Divine Voice announced that all who attended his funeral were destined for the World-to-Come, and the launderer, who came daily, had not come that day.
15.turn: When he heard the news he was overcome with grief and climbed to a roof and threw himself down, dying.
15.outcome: A Divine Voice announced that he too was destined for the World-to-Come.
15.summary: On the day of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's funeral a heavenly voice said that everyone who attended was destined for the World-to-Come. A launderer who visited Rabbi every day had not come that day. When he heard of the death and the announcement, he climbed to the roof, fell, and died, and the voice then declared that he too was destined for the World-to-Come.

16.event: He had interpreted every occurrence of the word et in the Torah as adding a law, until he reached the verse about fearing the Lord your God and stopped.
16.turn: His students asked what would become of all his earlier interpretations, and he said he was rewarded for withdrawing as he had been for expounding.
16.outcome: Rabbi Akiva later taught that this et includes Torah scholars.
16.summary: Shimon HaAmasoni used to draw extra laws from every et in the Torah, but he stopped when he reached the verse about fearing God, since nothing could be added to God's fear. His students asked what would happen to all his earlier teachings. He answered that he had been rewarded for expounding and was likewise rewarded for stopping. Rabbi Akiva later explained that the et there includes Torah scholars.

17.actor: A relative of Rav Nachman and her daughter
17.event: A relative of Rav Nachman sold her marriage contract, was divorced and then died, and the buyers demanded payment from her daughter.
17.turn: Rav Nachman asked aloud whether no one would advise the daughter, and then suggested she forgive her mother's marriage contract to her father and inherit it from him.
17.outcome: The daughter heard this, forgave the debt, and so avoided paying the buyers. Rav Nachman later regretted acting as an adviser to litigants.
17.summary: A relative of Rav Nachman sold her right to her marriage contract, was divorced and died. The buyers then claimed the money from her daughter. Rav Nachman said someone should tell the girl to forgive her father the debt so she could inherit it from him, and she went and did so. Rav Nachman later regretted having acted like an adviser to litigants.

18.event: Abaye's tenant farmer asked whether he could betroth a nursing woman after fifteen months, and Abaye gave him a lenient answer.
18.turn: Rav Yosef told Abaye that Rav and Shmuel required twenty-four months, so Abaye ran after the farmer to correct him.
18.outcome: He did not catch him, and Abaye concluded one should not rule in his teacher's presence.
18.summary: Abaye's tenant farmer asked if he could betroth a nursing woman after fifteen months, and Abaye told him he could. When Abaye told Rav Yosef, Rav Yosef cited Rav and Shmuel requiring twenty-four months. Abaye ran several parasangs after the farmer to stop him but did not catch him. He later said this showed one should not rule on even a simple matter near one's teacher.

19.event: Many men pressed to betroth her, and she told them she was already betrothed, then later betrothed herself to someone.
19.turn: The Sages asked why she did that, and she explained that she had said it to turn away unworthy suitors and acted when worthy ones came.
19.outcome: Rav Acha brought the case to the Sages at Usha, who ruled that if she gives a reason for her statement she is believed.
19.summary: A woman of great beauty was pursued by many men, and she told them she was already betrothed. Later she betrothed herself to one man. When the Sages asked why, she said she had turned away unworthy men and had accepted a worthy one. The Sages at Usha ruled that when a woman gives a reason for her statement she is believed.

20.event: Rabbi Abbahu was supported by two slaves in a bathhouse that collapsed, and Rabbi Yochanan was supported by two sages on a staircase that collapsed.
20.turn: Each of them found footing and pulled his supporters up, and the Sages asked why they needed support if they were so strong.
20.outcome: Rabbi Yochanan answered that he was saving his strength for his old age.
20.summary: Rabbi Abbahu stood in a bathhouse supported by two slaves when it collapsed. He climbed onto a pillar and pulled them up too. Rabbi Yochanan went up stairs with two sages supporting him, and when the stairs collapsed he climbed up and pulled them up as well. When asked why he needed support, he said he was saving his strength for old age.
